segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to Apphia our sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly that meets in your house:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank my God always when I mention you in my prayers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because I hear of your love and the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I pray that the partnership of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing that is in us for Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I have had great joy and encouragement from your love, because the hearts of the holy ones have been refreshed through you, brother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, although I have great boldness in Christ to command you to do what is fitting,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I appeal to you instead on the ground of love, being such as I am: Paul, an old man and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I appeal to you for my child, whose father I became in my chains: Onesimus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: once useless to you, but now useful both to you and to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am sending him back to you, him who is my very heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in my chains for the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your good deed would not be a matter of compulsion but of your own free will.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while: so that you might have him back for eternity,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if you hold me to be your partner, welcome him as you would me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it, not to mention that you owe me your very self besides.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I write to you confident of your obedience, knowing that you will do even more than I say.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the same time, prepare a guest room for me as well, for I hope that through your prayers I will be granted to you all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Epaphras, my fellow captive in Christ Jesus, greets you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is near-universal in English and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. Here the word refers to a group that met in a private home.

The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Some modern translations render it 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

notes.phrase: toward the Lord Jesus and for all the holy ones
notes.note: The Greek order is love, faith, the Lord Jesus, all the holy ones. Many interpreters read this as a crossed pattern: faith toward the Lord Jesus and love for all the holy ones, as in the parallel at Colossians 1:4. The translation keeps the Greek order and leaves the pairing open.

notes.traditional: the sharing of your faith; the communication of thy faith
notes.note: This verse is one of the most obscure in Paul's letters. The noun can mean partnership, participation, or generous sharing, so the phrase may mean Philemon's partnership with others in the faith, his share in the faith, or the generosity that springs from his faith. It almost certainly does not mean evangelism, as 'sharing your faith' suggests in modern English. 'Partnership' keeps the link with 'partner' in verse 17, which is a related Greek word.

The Greek word means the inner organs, regarded as the seat of the deepest feelings. Older versions have 'bowels', and 'heart' is the nearest modern equivalent. Paul uses the word three times in this short letter (verses 7, 12, 20), so that when he asks Philemon to 'refresh my heart' he is asking him to do for Paul what he already does for others.

The word normally means 'old man'. A nearly identical word means 'ambassador', and the two spellings were sometimes interchanged, so some scholars and a few translations read 'Paul, an ambassador and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus'. The manuscripts read 'old man', and that fits an appeal that sets aside authority.

notes.phrase: useless to you, but now useful
notes.note: Onesimus was a common slave name meaning 'useful' or 'profitable'. Paul plays on it with a different pair of Greek words for useless and useful: the man named Useful was once of no use and is now living up to his name.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

notes.traditional: he departed; he was parted from you
notes.note: Paul does not say Onesimus ran away. The passive verb leaves the cause unstated, and many interpreters see a hint that God's purpose lay behind the separation. The traditional view is that Onesimus was a runaway slave, but the letter never says so, and other reconstructions have been proposed, for example that he sought out Paul to intercede for him.

The Greek adjective 'eternal' is used here to describe how Philemon will have Onesimus back, in contrast to 'for a while' (literally 'for an hour'). English needs an adverbial phrase, so the noun form 'for eternity' stands in for the adjective. The word carries the sense of the age to come, a bond that outlasts the present life and not merely lifelong ownership.

The word meant a person owned by another, and first-century hearers understood it so. Older English versions have 'servant', and some modern ones 'bondservant', partly to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery. Several modern translations now use 'slave', and here the legal relationship of owner and slave is the subject of the letter.

notes.phrase: let me have this benefit from you
notes.traditional: let me have joy of thee; let me have some benefit from you
notes.note: The verb is related to the name Onesimus ('useful, beneficial') and occurs only here in the New Testament. It was a common idiom, so a deliberate pun cannot be proved. After the wordplay of verse 11, though, many interpreters think Paul is alluding to the name once more.
